title: The Roles of Placental Senescence, Autophagy and Senotherapeutics in the Development and Prevention of Pre-Eclampsia: A Focus on Ergothioneine
content: Cellular senescence is a well-established biological phenomenon in eukaryotes. It involves DNA damage, telomere shortening, a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), and the inability of cells to replicate. It is associated with ageing, and also with oxidative stress. Given the importance of oxidative stress in pre-eclampsia, there is considerable evidence, that we review, that senescence plays an important role in both normal placental development and in the development of both early- and late-term pre-eclampsia. Autophagy is capable of delaying or even reversing the development of senescence, and certain small molecules such as sulforaphane and spermidine can stimulate autophagy, including via the redox-sensitive transcription factor Nrf2. Ergothioneine is a thiohistidine antioxidant that is protective against a variety of cardiovascular and other diseases. Ergothioneine also interacts with Nrf2, and pre-eclampsia occurs far less frequently in individuals with higher plasma ergothioneine levels. Together, these elements provides a self-consistent, molecular and systems biology explanation for at least one mechanism by which ergothioneine may be protective against pre-eclampsia.
